data.sourceTitle: The Black Death: Causes and Spread
data.targetTitle: The Black Death: Causes and Spread
data.sourcePassage:
The Black Death was a pandemic that reached England in 1348. It was part of a much wider outbreak that had spread across Asia, the Middle East, North Africa and Europe. Modern historians and scientists link it to plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which could spread through fleas living on rodents and possibly through contact between people.

Medieval people, however, did not know about bacteria. They explained the disease using the knowledge and beliefs available to them. Many Christians believed plague was a punishment from God for sin. Others followed the miasma theory, which said that bad or corrupted air caused illness. Educated physicians sometimes blamed the alignment of planets, following the ideas of astrology. These explanations influenced how people tried to prevent disease — through prayer, burning herbs, carrying posies, or avoiding infected places.

The Black Death spread quickly because trade connected ports and towns across great distances. It probably arrived in England through southern ports such as Melcombe Regis in Dorset. From there it spread north and west. People who cared for the sick — family members, priests and nurses — were at risk because they had close contact with the dying. By 1349, the disease had moved through much of England.

Historians estimate that between one third and one half of England's population died, though exact figures are uncertain because medieval records are incomplete. The scale of death was unlike anything England had experienced before. Villages lost many of their inhabitants. Monasteries, hospitals and towns were severely affected. The Black Death left survivors in a world where normal life had been disrupted and the old social order would never be quite the same again.

questions.question: In which year did the Black Death arrive in England?
questions.modelAnswer: The Black Death arrived in England in 1348.

questions.question: What was the miasma theory?
options: The belief that plague was caused by bacteria
The belief that bad or corrupted air caused disease
The belief that fleas on rats spread illness
The belief that sin caused all physical suffering
questions.modelAnswer: Miasma theory was the belief that bad or corrupted air caused disease.

questions.question: Why did the Black Death spread quickly across England?
options: Because medieval people had modern germ theory and ignored it
Because trade routes connected ports and towns, and carers had close contact with the sick
Because the government deliberately spread the disease
Because England had no towns or cities at the time
questions.modelAnswer: The Black Death spread quickly because trade connected ports and towns, and people caring for the sick had close contact with the dying.

questions.question: Why is it historically unfair to say medieval people were 'stupid' for believing in miasma?
options: Because miasma was actually the correct scientific explanation
Because medieval people worked with the knowledge available to them and had no access to germ theory
Because medieval people never tried any treatments for plague
Because modern historians have proved miasma caused the Black Death
questions.modelAnswer: It is unfair because medieval people used the best knowledge available to them. Without microscopes or germ theory, miasma was a reasonable explanation within their world of ideas.

data.sourceTitle: The Impact of the Black Death on Medieval Society
data.targetTitle: The Impact of the Black Death on Medieval Society
data.sourcePassage:
The death of so many people caused by the Black Death transformed the economic relationship between landowners and workers in medieval England. Before the plague, landowners had plenty of workers available. After 1348, with so many dead, there were far fewer people to plough fields, tend livestock and manage estates. This created a labour shortage.

The surviving workers understood that their labour was now scarce and valuable. Some demanded higher wages. Some refused unpaid labour services. Others moved to different manors where lords offered better terms. Landowners, who had previously relied on cheap and controlled villein labour, found themselves competing for workers.

The government responded with the Statute of Labourers in 1351. This law tried to keep wages at pre-plague levels and prevent workers from moving in search of better pay. Employers who offered higher wages could be punished, as could workers who refused to accept old rates. The law shows that the ruling classes were alarmed. If workers could freely bargain for better conditions, the old social hierarchy might weaken.

However, passing a law was not the same as enforcing it perfectly. Many workers still found ways to negotiate. Local officials applied the law unevenly. The economic reality of scarce labour was difficult to ignore. The Statute of Labourers is historically important not only because of what it tried to do, but because it reveals the tension between economic change and the desire of powerful groups to preserve their position. It also contributed to growing resentment that would, over the following decades, help fuel the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

questions.question: What was the Statute of Labourers?
options: A law giving workers the right to higher wages
A law that tried to keep wages at pre-plague levels
A law abolishing villeinage
A law allowing workers to move freely between manors
questions.modelAnswer: The Statute of Labourers was a 1351 law that tried to keep wages at pre-plague levels and prevent workers from moving for better pay.

questions.question: Why did surviving workers have more bargaining power after the Black Death?
options: Because the government gave them more rights
Because landowners had lost all their money
Because their labour was scarce and landowners competed for workers
Because the Church supported higher wages
questions.modelAnswer: Workers had more bargaining power because their labour was scarce — with so many dead, landowners competed for the surviving workers.

questions.question: What does the passage of the Statute of Labourers suggest about how landowners felt after the Black Death?
options: They were happy for workers to earn higher wages
They were alarmed that the old social hierarchy might weaken
They believed the Black Death had no economic consequences
They wanted to abolish the manor system
questions.modelAnswer: The Statute shows landowners were alarmed that workers' newfound bargaining power threatened the old social hierarchy.

questions.question: How did the Statute of Labourers contribute to the causes of the Peasants' Revolt?
options: It gave rebels new legal rights to organise
It increased resentment by trying to stop workers benefiting from the labour shortage
It raised wages too quickly and destabilised the economy
It removed all taxes on peasants, making them ungrateful
questions.modelAnswer: The Statute increased resentment by trying to stop workers from benefiting from the labour shortage that the Black Death had created, building anger over decades that contributed to the 1381 revolt.

data.sourcePassage:
The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was one of the largest popular uprisings in medieval English history. It had several connected causes. The Black Death had created a labour shortage, raising workers' expectations. The Statute of Labourers tried to stop wages rising. Poll taxes introduced in 1377, 1379 and 1380 added financial pressure on ordinary households. The 1380 poll tax was particularly hated. When tax collectors investigated non-payment, local anger boiled over, first in Essex and then in Kent.

Wat Tyler became the leader of the Kentish rebels. Rebels marched towards London, and some Londoners opened the city gates to them. In London, rebels attacked symbols of royal government and officials they blamed for misrule. Richard II, who was about fourteen years old at the time, met the rebels at Mile End on 14 June 1381. He appeared to agree to their main demands, including ending villeinage and granting freedom to work for wages. Some rebels left London believing they had won.

The next day, at Smithfield, Richard met Wat Tyler again. During this tense encounter, Tyler was killed — by London's mayor, according to most accounts. Richard addressed the crowd and calmed the situation. Over the following weeks, royal forces crushed remaining revolts across the country. The promises Richard had made were cancelled. John Ball and other rebel leaders were executed.

In the short term, the revolt had clearly failed. However, historians debate its long-term significance. Villeinage continued to decline in the decades that followed, though this was partly due to the ongoing economic effects of the Black Death. The revolt showed that ordinary people could organise, march on London and force a king to negotiate. Whatever its immediate failure, it became an important symbol of popular protest against unfair government.

questions.question: Where did Wat Tyler meet his death on 15 June 1381?
options: Mile End
Smithfield
Westminster
Canterbury
questions.modelAnswer: Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield during a meeting with Richard II on 15 June 1381.

questions.question: Name two demands the rebels made at Mile End.
options: Lower poll taxes and more monasteries
An end to villeinage and freedom to work for wages
Higher poll taxes and land redistribution
Execution of the king and abolition of the Church
questions.modelAnswer: At Mile End the rebels demanded an end to villeinage and the freedom to work for wages.

questions.question: Why were the poll taxes of 1377–1380 a significant cause of the revolt?
options: They gave money directly to the rebels to fund the uprising
They placed financial pressure on ordinary households and provoked anger when collectors investigated non-payment
They were only paid by nobles, who then became angry
They abolished villeinage, which angered landowners into rebellion
questions.modelAnswer: The poll taxes placed financial pressure on ordinary households, and when tax collectors investigated non-payment, local anger ignited the revolt.

questions.question: Why do historians debate whether the Peasants' Revolt was a failure?
options: Because all rebels escaped punishment
Because the revolt succeeded in abolishing villeinage immediately
Because although it failed in the short term, villeinage continued to decline and it became a symbol of popular protest
Because Richard II kept all his promises to the rebels
